Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn President Nicușor Dan promulgated the law establishing 2026 as the Year of the United States of America in Romania on Monday, July 20. The bill was initiated by several lawmakers from the far-right, Eurosceptic but pro-Trump Alliance for the Union of Romanians party, or AUR. According to the law set to be implemented, 2026 is the Year of the United States of America in Romania. As such, events may be organized to strengthen the Romanian-American strategic relationship and reaffirm Romania's commitment to the values of the free world, freedom of expression, and genuine democracy, according to the law cited by Digi24 . To mark the celebration, central and local public administration authorities may organize or provide material or logistical support, within the limits of the approved budget allocations, for the organization and holding of conferences and public debates; cultural, academic and educational events dedicated to American history and values; Romanian-American public diplomacy and communication activities; any other activities promoting Romanian-American cooperation and democratic values. In addition, the Romanian Public Radio Broadcasting Company and the Romanian Public Television Company may broadcast thematic materials produced on the occasion of the Year of the United States of America in Romania. https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text: The new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England. Photograph: Peter Muller/Getty Images/Image Source View image in fullscreen The new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England. Photograph: Peter Muller/Getty Images/Image Source GCSEs Pupils to be offered vocational GCSEs in radical shake-up of system in England Courses such as finance and construction form part of PM’s push for education ‘that offers a path for everybody’ Richard Adams and Sally Weale Wed 23 Sep 2026 17.30 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Teenagers are to be offered a range of new vocational GCSEs under a radical shake-up of the school system in England designed to tackle a crisis that has left nearly a million young people out of work or training. From 2029, pupils will be able to supplement compulsory GCSE subjects such as English, maths and sciences with courses such as construction, creative media production and child development, marking the biggest changes to the qualification for more than a decade. The Department for Education (DfE) said the new GCSEs would be two-year courses taken in year 10 and 11, “with nationally set content, grading and assessment” and regulated by Ofqual, England’s qualifications watchdog, to the same standards as academic GCSEs. England’s teenagers outperform peers in most countries in maths, reading and science Read more The courses are part of an effort by Andy Burnham to fulfil his pledge of “an education system that offers a path for everybody, academic and technical, in equal balance”, made the day after his election as MP for Makerfield. Announcing the new courses, the prime minister said: “We’ve all heard someone say ‘school wasn’t really for me’ because they were not given the chance to study vocational courses as well as traditional subjects. “That one-size-fits-all approach isn’t working, so we’re building an education system that values both academic and technical paths. I want to give all young people across Britain the hope that their future will be brighter, whether it starts at university or not.” Whitehall sources said the courses were expected to be offered from September 2029 but that the education secretary, Lucy Powell, wanted to move more quickly if possible, with schools given the option to add vocational GCSEs to their existing subjects. Powell said: “Time and again young people, parents and employers tell me they want schools to do more to help them understand and prepare for the jobs of the future. Our new vocational GCSEs will give young people a stronger connection to the careers and industries shaping our economy, helping them discover and develop their talents while maintaining high standards across our education system. “This is not about creating different routes for different children. It is about ensuring every child has access to a rich and ambitious education that opens doors, creates opportunity and prepares them for life beyond the classroom.” View image in fullscreen The new courses would be designed to lead into further study including A-levels. Photograph: sturti/Getty Images The change is part of a range of measures that Burnham has announced since coming to power to tackle the Neets crisis, with a call to “value the hard hat as much as the graduation cap”. It follows plans to give local businesses a role in setting curriculums in their areas. In a review published in May, Alan Milburn said that without significant change the number of young people not in work or education could grow by 25% by the early 2030s, opening up a “generational fault line” between the young and old. Critics, however, say the focus on technical education risks widening the gap between richer and poorer children. Sam Freedman, a policy adviser to Michael Gove when he was education secretary, wrote last month : “The more we ration a full set of academic GCSEs to children from better-off families, the more we will bake in existing inequalities.” The shadow education secretary, Laura Trott, said the courses would mean lowered expectations for disadvantaged children who had benefited most from high standards. “Labour are sabotaging young people’s futures,” she said. “Just weeks after the latest Pisa results showed England’s pupils climbing into the world’s top 10 for reading, maths and science, they want to rip up the system and review existing GCSEs. “Soaring up international league tables didn’t happen by accident. It followed years of evidence-led reform built around knowledge, rigour and high expectations. Labour risks throwing that progress away and if English, maths and science become merely a ‘common entitlement’, not a requirement for new qualifications, we risk repeating the mistakes of the past.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The DfE said the subjects offered could include management and finance, creative media production, digital technology and building and construction, and would be designed to lead into further study including A-levels. The new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England, with travel and tourism and health and care courses among the most popular. About 350,000 technical awards and certificates were issued this year, compared with more than 5m GCSEs. Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needs Read more School leaders said the success of the new courses would depend on having the resources and staffing to teach specialist subjects. The general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, Pepe Di’Iasio, said: “Reshaping and rebadging vocational and technical qualifications is well intentioned but will not in itself address the barriers to more young people taking these subjects. Reform needs to be accompanied by a strategy to ensure that schools have the staffing and resources to deliver them, and a campaign to raise public awareness of vocational and technical routes.” The general secretary of the National Education Union, Daniel Kebede, agreed. “These proposed changes will fall at the first hurdle unless there is sufficient investment in schools and the workforce,” he said. The general secretary of the NAHT school leaders’ union, Paul Whiteman, said: “In recent years, the content behind too many GCSEs became unwieldy and the over-reliance on final exams did not play to the strengths of all students. “It will be crucial these pitfalls are avoided in developing these qualifications and that the government works closely with educators, local leaders and employers to ensure they offer high-quality learning which sets young people up for future training, education or employment.” The government has also said it will launch a “national mission” by calling on employers to provide an additional 200,000 work experience placements to give young people exposure to the workplace by age 16. No 10 North will offer work experience for students aged 14 to 16 this academic year. https://www.christiandaily.com/opinion/t.text: Anti-money laundering is often cited by governments restricting receipt of foreign funding by NGOs, but in South Asia controls are much more severe. India leads the way and has been suffocating the the flow of supply to many charitable causes for some time, Christian NGOs especially. This action goes far beyond accepted international standards and the right to appropriate international fund sharing should be contested in South Asian courts. Panida Wijitpanya/iStock Four South Asian states, four different legal vocabularies, one converging outcome: a civil society organization's ability to receive money from abroad is treated not as an incident of the right to associate, but as a permission the state may grant, withhold, or withdraw at will. South Asian states India now requires every recipient organization to bank through a single, government-designated branch in New Delhi. India's model is the region's best known. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, tightened substantially in 2020. India now requires every recipient organization to bank through a single, government-designated branch in New Delhi, it bars any transfer of foreign funds to another organization at all, and gives the state power to suspend a registration for up to a year before any final finding is made. More than sixteen thousand NGO registrations have been cancelled over the past decade. When the Supreme Court tested this framework in Noel Harper v Union of India (2022), it accepted the government's own submission virtually without qualification. The Court agreed that no organization has an inherent right to receive foreign contributions. More than sixteen thousand NGO registrations have been cancelled over the past decade. Nepal's architecture looks different on paper and, in one respect, is even more exacting. Under the Social Welfare Council Act and the Foreign Aid Policy, an NGO does not simply register once and comply thereafter; it must submit each individual foreign-funded project to the Social Welfare Council for prior approval. An NGO must then secure a further sign-off from the Ministry of Finance, before a single rupee may lawfully arrive. Approval precedes the transaction rather than following it; prior restraint is built directly into the ordinary course of funding, not reserved for exceptional cases. Pakistan... every international NGO... must seek fresh government approval before accepting funding from any new source or opening any new office. Pakistan combines registration with a security-clearance apparatus that extends beyond either. Under the 2015 Ministry of Interior policy, every international NGO must be cleared by a multi-agency committee that includes the country's principal intelligence services. They sign a memorandum of understanding, but then must seek fresh government approval before accepting funding from any new source or opening any new office, a standing requirement of prior permission for each subsequent transaction, not a one-time registration. It is worth setting this beside the law most frequently invoked as the Western precedent for this kind of regulation, the United States' Foreign Agents Registration Act, which requires registration and public disclosure but not prior government approval of who may fund an organization or when. Pakistan's regime is not a regional echo of FARA. It goes considerably beyond it. Sri Lanka... a bill.. drafted with heavy involvement from the Ministry of Public Security. Sri Lanka has not yet finished writing its own version of this story, and the drafting process is instructive in its own right. The country currently regulates NGOs under a fragmented, decades-old framework, but a new Non-Governmental Organizations Bill, drafted with heavy involvement from the Ministry of Public Security. The bill has had minimal consultation of the civil society groups it would govern, has been pending since 2024 and, tellingly, is being defended and debated in Colombo by direct reference to India's example. A recent Sri Lankan civil society commentary explicitly warned that "India's tightened Foreign Contribution Regulation Act has forced thousands of NGOs to close," citing India not necessarily as a cautionary outlier but certainly as the visible endpoint of a path that Sri Lanka's own drafters appear willing to walk. The region's states are not arriving at this architecture independently. They are watching and, in some cases, citing one another. International law Access to funding, including from abroad, falls within the protection of (UN) Article 22. Set against this pattern, international law's position is considerably narrower than any of these four regimes acknowledges. The UN Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly and of Association has stated plainly that access to funding, including from abroad, falls within the protection of Article 22 of the ICCPR. The UN argues that there exists a presumption in favor of the legality of an NGO's funding activities that the state, not the organization, bears the burden of displacing. The Financial Action Task Force, the very body most often invoked to justify these laws, revised its own standard in 2016 specifically to remove language casting the entire non-profit sector as inherently vulnerable, insisting instead on regulation targeted at organizations identified through documented, individualized risk assessment. Concerns about money laundering. The Venice Commission has drawn the line with particular clarity: concerns about money laundering may justify enhanced reporting, but never an outright ban on ordinary fund transfers of the kind India's Section 7 and Pakistan's approval regime both impose. And where comparable laws have actually been tested in court outside the region, they have not survived contact with a serious proportionality analysis. The Court of Justice of the European Union struck down Hungary's transparency law in 2020, and the European Court of Human Rights found Russia's foreign-agent framework disproportionate in 2022, in both cases rejecting sovereignty and transparency as sufficient justification on their own. South Asia's foreign-funding laws are not converging toward that baseline. They are converging away from it, each new statute citing the last as evidence that the approach is normal rather than as a warning that it is not. Breaking that cycle will require courts willing to ask the question their counterparts elsewhere have already asked, not whether a state may regulate foreign funding, which nobody disputes, but whether the specific mechanism chosen is necessary, proportionate, and actually justified by evidence rather than by the mere fact that a neighboring state has already done the same. Robin Christopher Joseph serves as Legal Counsel at ADF International , supporting legal and advocacy initiatives across Asia relating to freedom of religion or belief, freedom of expression and other fundamental rights. He holds an LL.M. from Azim Premji University, completed coursework in International Human Rights Law at the University of Oxford, and earned his law degree from Christ University. https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/front/a.text: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home Front Page Eleven missing after drones hit ships off Bulgaria AFP, SOFIA Add TT as Preferred Source Eleven people are missing after two merchant ships were yesterday struck by drones off Bulgaria in the latest spillover from the Ukraine war in the Black Sea. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev summoned the Russian ambassador after drones struck a Ukrainian-owned cargo ship, while another vessel was also hit and sank further north off the coast of the NATO and EU member. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the alliance would adjust its defenses “as needed.” Emergency personnel help the crew of the Chelsea 3 after it was hit by drones near Byala, Bulgaria, yesterday. Photo: Bulgarian Ministry of Interior via AP The Ukrainian-owned cargo ship Chelsea 3 was “hit by three aerial drones,” and shortly afterward another ship was “struck” and sank, Radev said. “We lack solid, clear evidence to level accusations against any specific party; however ... logic suggests the outcome works to the advantage of the Russian Federation,” he wrote, calling the attack “unacceptable.” The presidency later identified the ship that sank as the HS Dignity , a Guinea-Bissau flagged cargo vessel that was en route to the Romanian port of Braila It went down 17 nautical miles (31.5km) east of the Krapets, Bulgaria. “According to information we got from the rescue center ... five people were rescued and 11 are missing. This is preliminary information,” a spokeswoman for the northeastern region of Dobrich said. All 15 crew members aboard the stricken Chelsea 3 — seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis — had been rescued after it was hit 18 nautical miles east of Byala, Bulgaria, Radev said. Rutte, speaking after a call with Radev, said NATO would continue to work closely “with our allies in the Black Sea.” “We have already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank and will continue to monitor the security environment, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed,” Rutte wrote. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the latest attacks, calling them “another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine.” Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andriy Sybiga also blamed Russia, denouncing what he called Moscow’s “deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea.” “The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponize hunger and hold the world hostage,” he wrote on X. Amid mounting fallout from Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, drone attacks have become increasingly frequent in neighboring countries. The conflict has also spread across the eastern Black Sea, with at least 45 merchant vessels attacked over the past 12 months in areas previously not listed as high risk, the maritime risk management group Ambrey said last month. No strikes were recorded in the areas in the preceding 12 months, Ambrey said, adding that the increase was driven by attacks further from the coasts of Russia and Ukraine. Last week, two commercial vessels were hit in the Black Sea off Bulgaria in an attack widely blamed on Russia, although Bulgaria said the circumstances were unclear. Nine Syrians and one Egyptian remain missing. That dual strike came a day after another ship caught fire and sank off the Romanian coast, killing one person and leaving another missing. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said the ship was hit by Russian drones. https://www.wvik.org/wvik-top-stories/20.text: On Air Now Playing WVIK News On Air Now Playing WVIK Classical On Air Now Playing APRIS News Durbin, Sorensen tour growing Moline defense contractor WVIK, Quad Cities NPR | By Jonathan Turner Published October 29, 2026 at 9:32 PM CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 1:39 Jonathan Turner/WVIK News U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (D-Moline), center, and U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) look at a part produced by ASTRO America Midwest, during a plant open house at their Moline facility, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. A growing Moline-based company was the focus of a tour Thursday, Oct. 29 for U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) and U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (D-Moline). Applied Science and Technology Research Organization of America (ASTRO America) held an Advanced Manufacturing Open House with the two elected officials, and leaders from the aerospace and defense manufacturing community. ASTRO leaders and employees displayed parts of the existing Moline facility, showed examples of large-scale metal additive manufacturing, and talked of the plans for a new 25,000-square-foot Center for Solid State Manufacturing, currently under development in Milan. The Quad Cities was also hailed for its growing role as a hub for advanced manufacturing, highlighting ASTRO America’s work with the U.S. Army to develop next-generation production technologies and strengthen the nation's defense. Since January 2023, ASTRO America Midwest has operated in a 5,500-square-foot warehouse building, 3200 69 th Ave., near the QC International Airport, Moline. The company plans to invest $20 million to open in a 25,000-square-foot building in Milan this February, said Neal Orringer, CEO of ASTRO America and a former Department of Defense Director of Manufacturing. Jonathan Turner/WVIK News Noah Barnhill (left), manager of the ASTRO America facility at 3200 69th Ave., Moline, explains their process to U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin and U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen during a tour Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. “We needed a true manufacturing hub to demonstrate technology's utility to our warfighter. And there's no better place to do that than Rock Island, and there's no better folks to do it than the Rock Island personnel, the folks who work in manufacturing,” Orringer said Thursday. “There's also no better champion than Senator Durbin. for Rock Island Arsenal. Through his legislation, the Army Arsenal Strategic Workload Enhancement Act, which was incorporated into the 2013 Defense Authorization Act, Centers of Industrial and Technical Excellence were created, and Rock Island was designated as the Army's Advanced Manufacturing Center of Excellence.” In 2020, ASTRO (which operates nationwide) partnered with RIA “to jumpstart an entire ecosystem that's now pioneering new advanced manufacturing technologies for defense production,” he said. “Rock Island Arsenal personnel are deploying this technology with their characteristic talents. And I want to thank our Rock Island partners for being here today,” Orringer said. “They're our most valued partner, and it takes a lot of hard work and patience to transition developmental machines for production, and nobody does it better. And we're not alone. Secretary Ash Carter, my, my old boss, used to say, DOD doesn't design and make our weapon systems, they come from our defense industry. "And together with our men and women in uniform, that's what makes the U.S. military power unrivaled. So in 2021, ASTRO turned to the defense industry to demonstrate viability of additive friction stir deposition for weapon system production.” ASTRO produces parts for General Dynamics, Boeing, and BAE Systems for military planes, helicopters, tanks and other ground vehicles. Jonathan Turner/WVIK News ASTRO America employees explain their jobs to U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin and U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen during a tour of the company's Moline facility, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. “Quad Cities is now a hub for 3D aerospace production. Make no mistake about that,” Orringer said, noting that’s based on four facts -- Rock Island Arsenal's part producers; ASTRO’s manufacturing research engineers; metal fabrication companies in the area, and “the nation's leading aerospace producers, all convening here in the Quad Cities, driving innovation, economic development, and more and more high-skilled jobs,” he said. ASTRO America supports collaborations by government agencies and companies to address supply chain challenges in highly regulated industries, including aerospace and defense. What’s the need for expansion? Driving the need for expansion (moving to a much bigger facility) is to have the whole process (design, build, test) under one roof, to be able to produce and test larger parts and more of them, Orringer said. “One of the most important things that we're trying to establish is we're not just building experimental 3D printing technology just to advance the science. The goal is to really validate this technology and make sure that it can be repeatable and actually get it into a supply chain,” he said. “In order to do that, you need to test the heck out of these parts. It's hard to find metrology tools and other kinds of characterization tools that are large enough to actually handle. So we have to have ultrasound, X-ray, CT scanners, and other kinds of technology to validate the quality of the build. Jonathan Turner/WVIK News Neal Orringer, CEO of ASTRO America (which has three facilities in the U.S. and one in Guam), speaks at a press conference in Moline, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. “So we're not only going to have production capability, but we're now building some of the largest metrology equipment. So we're going to have a massive ultrasound immersion tank. It'll be one of the biggest in the country,” Orringer said. “Now you'll have to get a big forklift to get it over there and put it in that immersion tank, but that won't fit in a space like this. So we had to grow into something a little bigger.” “Think of ASTRO America as a corporate laboratory. We are helping develop the process for manufacturing,” he said. “The JMTC, the Rock Island Arsenal, they are a critical production plant. So our job is to make sure that this technology is ready for primetime, ready for folks to actually use this technology to get parts into the field. And that's why we're really grateful for the opportunity to partner with JMTC.” ASTRO perfects the parts, which are mass produced at the Arsenal. “They’re doing higher-scale part production, and our job is to run through the process development, figure out a roadmap for how to do production right,” Orringer said. “We're trying to figure out what is the right kind of data to collect as you're building the parts so that we can figure out how to course correct when there's a need.” ASTRO is filling a key manufacturing need since there’s very limited amount of metal forging capacity in the U.S., declining by 50% in the last several years. Jonathan Turner/WVIK News Company CEO Neal Orringer is a former director of manufacturing for The Pentagon. “How do we make up for that? We're not going to necessarily be able to foot the bill to the tens, if not hundreds of millions of dollars, build more forging capacity in the United States,” Orringer said. “And it's critical that we have domestic capabilities, particularly for U.S. defense needs, but also for aerospace and other things. So being able to get a replacement for forging, whether it's for aerospace or for rockets or for any other kind— shipbuilding— that's what we're really gearing towards.” There are a number of metal 3D printing companies across the country, and ASTRO is unique since this technology, “instead of using a heat source, it's using friction to actually combine different layers. And so this particular kind of metal system is uniquely suited for large-scale metal that will hopefully be a suitable alternative,” he said. “Our goal is to figure out how to transition this equipment from being something that's been generally used in a laboratory into a production environment. And that's what we're hoping we can do with critical partners like Boeing and the Army,” Orringer said, noting ASTRO will hire new employees for Milan, though he didn’t know exactly how many (there are 15 now in Moline). “We've already begun a new project where we're not only working with Boeing on helicopter components, but also Sikorsky, who's another big helicopter company, and Bell,” Orringer said. “So you could potentially see us hopefully finding a way for making parts for the Apache helicopter, the Black Hawk helicopter, and some next-generation helicopter. And then also maybe there's some commercial opportunities beyond the Army, maybe some other kinds of aerospace.” Back from Romania Congressman Eric Sorensen, a member of the Armed Services Committee, recently returned from Romania and the Black Sea, where Ukrainian fighter pilots are being trained by American fighter pilots. They said they can’t use all their F-16s because they sometimes need to swap out parts from one plane to the other. Jonathan Turner/WVIK News Congressman Eric Sorensen speaking at Thursday's press conference at ASTRO America, Moline. “That's how important what we do here in the Quad Cities is. not just for us as an economic driver in the Quad Cities and in the state of Illinois, but it's about how we support our warfighters for peace around the world,” Sorensen said. “Being here at ASTRO shows that our commitment to the Quad Cities being forever connected to the Rock Island Arsenal and the United States Army,” he said, crediting Durbin’s legacy of service and support for national defense. “When you're Dick Durbin, everybody knows your commitment to the Arsenal. So we get to do some really, really great things for this community. And quite literally, we would not have JMTC (at the Arsenal) and advanced manufacturing here if you, Dick Durbin, didn't champion it for years and years and years.” “Today we're pushing the bounds of what we considered impossible just years ago, and that's why I'm excited about what's coming next and for what will happen soon in the city of Milan,” Sorensen said. “The new facility will only further cement the Quad Cities region as a nation-driving innovator for 3D printing and advanced manufacturing.” Honoring Durbin’s legacy Orringer presented Sen. Durbin (who’s retiring effective January 2027, after 44 years in Congress) an ASTRO-produced replica of a vehicle wheel hub that goes on a combat vehicle, in thanks for his work. Jonathan Turner/WVIK News ASTRO America CEO Neal Orringer presented U.S. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) with an ASTRO-produced replica of a military vehicle wheel hub on Thursday, in gratitude for his decades-long support of the Rock Island Arsenal and defense community in the region. “I was told at the outset that the Arsenal was doomed. It wasn't going to last. But it turned out they were wrong,” Durbin said Thursday. “It wasn't enough to have a clout-heavy senator in Washington or even have the local communities all together. We had to do something that would defend the United States, because that ultimately is why the Arsenal exists, to make sure that we are a safer country. “What you see here was beyond anything I could have even described when I started in this effort,” he said of ASTRO. “I knew that innovation in manufacturing and innovation in processing could make us unique, and we're proving that we have been. As I talked to some of our friends from the military about situation at the Arsenal. I talked about this process and we're talking and I said, is this unique? And you said yes, there's no other Arsenal in the United States that has this.” “Thank you for this award. And I hope the good work of the Arsenal does more than create a good story for history. I hope it creates a path for the future that makes us a safer nation,” Durbin added. Jonathan Turner / WVIK News U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin is retiring this January, after 44 years in Congress, including the last 30 in the Senate. “Astro is a recognized entity that tests for the very best, and the Arsenal is tied to that testing,” he said later. “Today, this tour that I took would have been unthinkable back then, 40 years ago. Some of the things we discussed today weren't even in the realm of possibility. “But now they're in the realm of not only for the possibility, but timeliness in terms of the future of the Arsenal,” Durbin said. “We have a unique production facility on the island for the Arsenal. It's going to be used to make parts for aircraft and submarines. It's going to keep them functional and keep our troops safe. That's what we need more than ever.” Durbin honored at Arsenal lunch During an earlier lunch Thursday convened by Quad Cities elected officials, Army leaders, and local defense industry partners, the Rock Island Arsenal Defense Alliance (RIADA) and the Quad Cities Manufacturing Institute (QCMI) each presented Durbin with an award in honor of his decades of public service and his support for the Rock Island Arsenal and local defense community. Durbin has been a strong partner to both RIADA and QCMI in securing federal funding for the region’s defense manufacturing industry, including in support of QCMI research with the Army in fiscal years 2024 and 2026. He has been integral in securing federal funding for the Arsenal’s 3D jointless hull printer, which is the largest metal 3D printer in the world. “I’m grateful to the Rock Island Arsenal Defense Alliance, the Quad Cities Manufacturing Institute, and ASTRO America for this recognition, and more importantly, being my partner in supporting the men and women at the Rock Island Arsenal,” Durbin said in a Thursday release from his office. “You all help ensure the Arsenal and the Quad Cities remain an integral part of helping Illinois lead the future of manufacturing, using cutting-edge technology at crisis speed,” he said. “It has been the honor of a lifetime to do my part over the years in Congress, working side by side with you to secure hundreds of millions of dollars each year in federal investments to modernize Rock Island Arsenal and safeguard its future. I know that when the next call comes from our nation and our military, the Arsenal will once again be ready to answer.” This story was produced by WVIK, Quad Cities NPR.
